Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Open with the care line: a prescription is treatment, and it’s yours. Keep the line on borrowed pills, never on students who take their own.

Slide 10 · Notes

Adderall and Ritalin raise dopamine and norepinephrine. Dopamine makes dull work feel interesting and helps hold the plan. Norepinephrine makes you feel wired and pushes heart rate up. Ask: if boring work feels interesting, how would you know you learned more?

Slide 11 · Notes

An ADHD brain often starts low, and the right dose moves it up. A brain without ADHD usually starts near the top; extra pushes it over the hump. A model from brain research, not a measure of any one person. It’s also why prescribed medication works for the person it was prescribed to.

Slide 12 · Notes

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why a borrowed stimulant feels like it's working, what the research shows about actual scores, and which study habits really do raise them. Students with ADHD prescriptions should leave feeling respected, never suspected.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards for the exit card
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minHelps, hurts, or meh? (fingers vote)
  2. 6 minThe circuit stimulants push on
  3. 4 minThe hill: why more isn’t better
  4. 8 minThree research guesses
  5. 4 minThe costs
  6. 4 minFeels productive, isn’t: turn and talk, share out
  7. 8 minThree situations: Claire, Theo, Max
  8. 3 minThe real performance stack
  9. 3 minEvery student, exit card

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Two of the votes, the hill, the 13-test guess, one situation, and the real stack.

Before you teach
Protect students who take their own medication.

Say early and plainly: prescribed medication for ADHD is legitimate treatment, at the dose a doctor set. Nobody owes the class a reason for taking it.

Don't ask who has a prescription.

Not by show of hands, not by glance. Pressure on students with prescriptions to share or sell is part of what this lesson is trying to ease.

Expect pushback on "it doesn't work."

Students will say it helped them. Agree that the focus feeling is real. The research question is whether scores moved, and in blinded studies they mostly didn't.

Name the pressure.

Heavy course loads, jobs and short sleep are real. Treat the shortcut as an understandable idea that doesn't deliver, and spend time on what does.

If a student is being pressured or is buying.

Thank them and connect them with a counselor that day. A counselor can help without making them the story.

Know the emergency signs.

Chest pain, a pounding heart that won't slow, fainting, seizure, very high temperature, or extreme panic after a stimulant: 911. A pill that didn't come from a pharmacy plus someone very sleepy or hard to wake could be fentanyl: 911 and naloxone.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

ADHD is a real diagnosis.

Neurodivergent students hear plenty of doubt about their meds. Keep every line about borrowed pills. An evaluation finds the actual reason and the right support, which might be medication, accommodations, coaching or a mix.

Families see ADHD differently.

Some see a medical question, some a matter of effort or faith, some worry about labels. A counselor can help a student raise an evaluation at home in a way that fits their family.

Access to evaluation.

Testing can be expensive and slow. Students whose families can't easily pay may see borrowing as the only option. Mention that the counselor can help with free or school-based routes.

Pressure looks different.

Some students carry heavy course loads because a family's sacrifices ride on their grades; some work weekends to help at home. Name both as real reasons for stress.

Learning support.

Students with a learning plan may feel singled out. Present "ask early" for extra help as something every student can do.

Mixed names and situations.

Use the scenario names as written. Avoid implying that any group of students is more likely to misuse pills.

What the research says

Dopamine's effect on working memory and control follows an upside-down U: too little or too much and the prefrontal cortex works worse.

Cools and D'Esposito, Biological Psychiatry, 2011

In a double-blind study, healthy young adults on Adderall didn't improve overall on 13 tests of memory, reasoning and creativity, but believed they had done better.

Ilieva, Boland and Farah, Neuropharmacology, 2013

40 adults without ADHD worked longer and made more moves on a hard planning puzzle after stimulants, and the quality of their answers dropped.

Bowman et al., Science Advances, 2023

Among 1,253 college first-years, students using stimulants without a prescription skipped more classes, studied less and had lower GPAs by year's end.

Arria et al., Journal of Drug Issues, 2008

Lifetime nonmedical stimulant use among 8th, 10th and 12th graders fell from about 10% in 2005 to under 5% in 2023.

McCabe et al., JAMA, 2025

Students who practiced recalling a passage remembered more a week later than students who reread it, even though rereading made them more confident.

Roediger and Karpicke, Psychological Science, 2006

Counterfeit pills pressed to look like Adderall increasingly contain methamphetamine or fentanyl and are often sold through social media.

U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, 2021
